title: Grace and free choice as two parts of one complete cause
source_text: LXXXIX. Igitur, ex illius mente, gratia Dei & liberum hominis arbitrium sunt duae partes unius integrae causae actus credendi, sperandi, aut poenitendi, prout ad salutem oportet; singulique ejusmodi actus pendent ab influxu tam liberi arbitrii, quam gratiae divinae: atque a libero quidem arbitrio habent, ut quoad substantiam sint credere, sperare, poenitere; ab influxu vero gratiae, ut sint supernaturales, & quales ad salutem sunt necessarii. Adeoque quivis eorum actuum, totus est a libero arbitrio, & totus a gratia: sed a neutro est ut a tota & integra causa, verum ut a parte integrae causae. Prout autor ille suam sententiam exponit, initio jamjam citatae disputationis.
pass_a_gloss: LXXXIX. Therefore, from his mind, the grace of God and the free choice of man are two parts of one whole cause of the act of believing, hoping, or repenting, as is needful for salvation; and each act of this kind depends on the influx as well of free choice, as of divine grace: and from free choice indeed they have, that as regards substance they be believing, hoping, repenting; but from the influx of grace, that they be supernatural, and such as are necessary for salvation. And so any of those acts, is wholly from free choice, and wholly from grace: but from neither as from the whole and entire cause, but as from part of the entire cause. As that author sets forth his opinion, at the beginning of the disputation just now cited.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXXIX. On his view, then, God's grace and man's free choice are two parts of one complete cause of the act of believing, hoping or repenting as salvation requires it, and each such act depends on the influence both of free choice and of divine grace. From free choice they have that in their substance they are believing, hoping and repenting; from the influence of grace, that they are supernatural and of the kind needed for salvation.

So each of these acts is wholly from free choice and wholly from grace, but from neither as from the whole and complete cause, only as from a part of the complete cause. This is how that author sets out his view at the beginning of the disputation just cited.
